pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: A sponsor says 'build photo sharing'. What two kinds of requirements do you extract before designing anything, and why do you explicitly mark some functional requirements as nice-to-have instead of just dropping them?
expected_points: functional (what the system does) vs non-functional (how well: scale, latency, availability, durability, cost)
must-have vs nice-to-have is scoping, and out-of-scope is a recorded decision, not a dismissal
non-functional requirements are what actually shape the architecture

questions.prompt: Walk me through estimating write QPS and yearly storage for an app with 10M registered users where people upload photos. What habits make the estimate trustworthy?
expected_points: state assumptions out loud: DAU share of registered, uploads per active user per day, bytes per upload
arithmetic chain: per-day totals divided by ~10^5 seconds/day, then a stated peak factor on top of average
round aggressively to powers of ten and sanity-check against an anchor or known system

questions.prompt: Why do the numbers come before the boxes? What does a five-minute envelope actually buy you?
expected_points: it reveals the dominant axis (read QPS, write QPS, storage, or bandwidth)
the dominant axis chooses where design effort and deep dives go
without numbers, architecture choices are vibes and can't be challenged or defended

questions.prompt: I claim storing images in object storage is simply best practice. Frame that properly as a trade-off for me.
expected_points: name at least two alternatives (e.g. blobs in the database vs object storage plus a metadata row)
attach costs to both sides, including the picked one (two systems can disagree; orphaned rows/objects)
tie the pick to a requirement or estimate, and state what would flip it (e.g. tiny low-volume images)

questions.prompt: You get 60 minutes to present a design. What are the five phases, in order, and which two habits keep the structure honest?
expected_points: requirements & scope, estimation, high-level architecture, deep dives, bottlenecks & evolution
drive with the numbers: estimation picks the deep dives
loop back when a deep dive uncovers a requirement question — the phases are a checklist, not one-way

questions.prompt: Why is 'nothing would change my decision' a red flag in a design review?
expected_points: designs fit requirements; if no requirement change flips the choice, it's dogma not analysis
the flip condition proves the alternatives were honestly costed
reviewers probe exactly there: when does the other option win?

questions.prompt: Two teams implement the identical feature list and produce wildly different architectures, both correctly. How?
expected_points: different non-functional requirements: scale, latency, availability, consistency, or cost targets
100 users vs 100 million turns the same functional spec into different problems
evaluating a design requires knowing its targets, not just its features
